title: Stock piled in discount-store escape routes and against final exits between daily checks: ~£10k-per-offence fire prosecutions
problem: Deliveries arrive faster than staff can shelve them, so cages and boxes end up in rear escape corridors and against final exit doors, usually on delivery days and between the daily paper 'exit walk'. Fire authorities prosecute under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005. Reported cases: JD Sports ~£10k per offence for six offences (one route cut to ~30cm); Poundstretcher ~£200k at one store and ~£1m in total; Tesco ~£95k plus costs (2010); B&M ~£33k. Repeat breaches are often found on revisit.
who_suffers: Store managers and staff; area managers who sign off compliance; customers and staff in a fire
buyer: Head of Health & Safety / Compliance Manager at a multi-site discount, variety or fashion retailer (20–500 stores)
industry: Discount, variety and fashion retail chains with rear stockrooms and back-of-house escape corridors
current_workaround: Paper daily fire-exit checklists, area-manager audits and occasional CCTV review. 'Blocked exit' camera-analytics packs (Hanwha, Axis) only work where AI cameras and store IT networks already exist.
sensor_concept: Battery ToF/mmWave distance sensor mounted above each final exit and corridor pinch point, measuring clear width. It flags any static object that stays more than 15 minutes, and a reed contact on the exit door adds context. LTE-M/LoRaWAN, no store IT. Push alert to the store manager with escalation to the area manager, plus an automatic daily exit-check record per store for the fire risk assessment and enforcement visits.
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong: named RRFSO prosecutions with £ figures. c2: daily check duty and weekly delivery-driven recurrence. c5: central H&S head owns fines and budget. c7: incumbents need AI CCTV plus IT, so a no-IT ~£30 node is a real gap. c8: ToF plus LPWAN. c6: fire-alarm and extinguisher maintainers already visit every store.

title: Independent jewellers can't prove the block-policy 'stock in safe out of hours' warranty after a break-in
problem: Jewellers' block policies typically require window and display stock to be cleared into a locked safe out of business hours, with the alarm set. After a burglary or smash-and-grab (~£20k–£250k of stock), the insurer asks what was left in the window and whether the safe was locked. If the warranty was breached, or can't be shown to have been met, the claim is cut or refused and renewal premiums jump. Financial Ombudsman decisions show block-policy disputes turning on what records the jeweller kept.
who_suffers: Owner of an independent jeweller; staff who close up at night
buyer: Owner/Managing Director of an independent jeweller or small jewellery chain (1–15 shops)
industry: Independent jewellers, watch dealers and pawnbrokers insured on jewellers' block policies
current_workaround: Paper close-down checklist, alarm set/unset reports from the monitoring company and manual stock counts. Nothing timestamps that the trays left the window and that the safe door was shut and bolted.
sensor_concept: Force-sensitive pressure pads under window and display trays (tray present or absent), a reed plus bolt-throw contact on the safe door, and a light sensor for window lighting. LTE-M with battery backup. Alert if trays are still in the window, or the safe is open, 15 minutes after the set closing time. Nightly time-stamped 'stock secured' certificate shared with the broker/insurer.
notes: c1: high stock losses per incident. c4: explicit insurer warranty, with FOS decisions as evidence. c5: owner holds both loss and budget. c6: specialist jewellers' block brokers/insurers and NSI alarm installers already serve these shops. c7: alarms log set/unset but not warranty compliance, so likely unserved. c8: FSR pads plus reed contacts, very cheap.

title: Shop fire extinguishers go missing, get used as door wedges or are let off between monthly checks
problem: BS 5306-3 expects the responsible person to visually inspect every portable extinguisher at least monthly, with a yearly service by a competent contractor. In busy stores, units are moved, stolen, discharged by youths or used to prop doors. Fire-safety enforcement notices and prosecutions routinely list missing, discharged or unserviced extinguishers among the breaches (combined fines ~£5k–£100k). Multi-site retailers cannot verify that the monthly check actually happens in each store.
who_suffers: Store managers and H&S teams; anyone who needs an extinguisher in a fire
buyer: Health & Safety Manager / Facilities Manager at a multi-site retailer or franchise group
industry: High-street, convenience and shopping-centre retail chains
current_workaround: Monthly paper tag checks by store staff and an annual BAFE contractor service at ~£10–£20 per unit, plus replacement charges after theft or discharge.
sensor_concept: Wall-bracket puck with hall/reed sensor (extinguisher present) and accelerometer (lifted, moved, discharged via sustained vibration), plus an optional ToF sensor facing out to detect blocked access. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT with 5-year battery. Instant alert on removal, and an auto-generated monthly inspection record per unit.
notes: c2: monthly duty per unit. c3: paid annual service plus staff time. c4: BS 5306-3 and RRFSO. c6: extinguisher service firms visit every site yearly and would resell. c7: a US incumbent (en-Gauge) exists, but UK SME retail looks unserved. c8: hall plus accelerometer. c1 is the weak point.

title: Blocked roof outlets on supermarket and retail-park flat roofs flood the sales floor in a cloudburst
problem: Leaves, nests and debris block siphonic and gravity outlets on large flat roofs. In summer thunderstorms water ponds, overtops upstands or brings ceilings down. Stores reported closed after rain came through the roof include Tesco Inverness (2022), Asda Sittingbourne, Morrisons Maidstone (2020) and Lidl Nottingham. A one-day superstore closure loses ~£100k+ of sales, on top of stock write-offs and ceiling repairs, and insurers ask for gutter-maintenance records.
who_suffers: Store managers, staff and customers; the retailer's property team
buyer: Regional Facilities / Property Maintenance Manager of a supermarket or discount chain, or the managing agent of a retail park
industry: Supermarkets, retail warehouses and retail parks with large flat or low-pitch roofs
current_workaround: Planned gutter and outlet clearance once or twice a year by roofing/gutter contractors, then reactive call-outs after a leak. Nobody watches the roof during the storm.
sensor_concept: Pressure-transducer or stacked float-switch water-depth sensor in each outlet sump or gutter bay, plus a tipping-bucket rain gauge on the roof. LTE-M, battery powered. Alert when depth keeps rising after rain stops (outlet blocked) or exceeds design head. Outlet-by-outlet 'clear now' list for the contractor, and a maintenance evidence log for insurers.
notes: c1/c10: store-closure losses with repeated news coverage. c6: roof/gutter contractors already visit on contract and could sell clear-on-demand. c8: float/pressure sensor plus LPWAN. c7: no niche product seen. c2 (several storms a year) and c4 (no explicit rule) are the weak points.

title: Aquatic retailers' shared tank systems lose a pump, heater or power overnight and the whole fish stock dies
problem: Independent aquatic shops and garden-centre aquatic departments run dozens of display tanks off shared sumps. A tripped pump, failed heater or power cut overnight can wipe out ~£5k–£30k of livestock by morning. Licences to sell animals as pets, under the Animal Welfare (Licensing of Activities Involving Animals) (England) Regulations 2018, require daily checks, suitable environmental monitoring and records. The inspector's star rating, and so the licence length and fee, depends on them.
who_suffers: Shop owner and aquatics staff; the livestock
buyer: Owner of an independent aquatic centre, or Aquatics Manager/concession holder in a garden-centre group
industry: Independent aquatic retailers and garden-centre aquatic departments (licensed pet sellers)
current_workaround: Staff checks at opening and closing, paper temperature logs for the licensing inspector, consumer aquarium controllers on a few tanks, and owners living nearby.
sensor_concept: Sealed DS18B20 temperature probes in each sump, current clamps on main return pumps and heater circuits, a float switch for sump low level, and mains-loss detection. LTE-M with battery backup, so no reliance on shop Wi-Fi. Out-of-hours phone/SMS alerts and auto-generated daily licence records.
notes: c1: stock loss per incident. c4: statutory licence conditions on daily checks and records. c5: owner-operator holds loss and budget. c6: livestock wholesalers deliver weekly, and licensing inspections happen regularly. c8: temperature, current and float only. c7: consumer controllers exist, but nothing multi-system with licence records.

title: Supermarket and retail-park car parks ice over before the gritter comes, leaving slip claims with no proof of treatment
problem: Retailers owe visitors a duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act. A customer slipping on black ice in a car park typically brings a claim of ~£3k–£20k, and the defence depends on showing the surface was monitored and treated. Gritting contractors either grit on a regional forecast trigger, billing per run (~£100–£300), or miss localised cold spots, and the retailer can't prove either way.
who_suffers: Customers and staff who fall; store managers; the retailer's claims team
buyer: Facilities Manager / Claims & Risk Manager of a supermarket chain or retail-park owner
industry: Supermarket, DIY and retail-park customer car parks and service yards
current_workaround: Forecast-triggered gritting contracts, staff spreading salt by hand, and photos plus paper gritting logs.
sensor_concept: Pole-mounted IR surface-temperature sensor (MLX90614-class) plus air temperature/humidity for dew point. LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Ice-risk alert per car park and a time-stamped log of surface conditions and treatment (contractor taps an NFC tag on arrival). Produces a winter claim-defence pack.
notes: c1: slip-claim values. c2: nightly through winter. c3: paid per-visit gritting. c6: gritting contractors already sell proof-of-service and would bundle. c8: cheap IR thermometer plus LPWAN. c4 rests on liability law rather than a check rule (risk).

title: Automatic sliding entrance doors close on elderly shoppers or stick open overnight between six-monthly services
problem: Store entrance doors cycle ~1,000+ times a day. Worn belts, misaligned safety sensors and failing operators cause doors to close on customers (injury claims ~£5k–£25k), stick open at night (a breach of the insurer's security conditions) or fail shut (lost trade). BS EN 16005 and the DHF code expect owner checks and competent periodic servicing, but servicing runs on the calendar and daily checks are rarely recorded.
who_suffers: Elderly and disabled customers; store managers; the retailer's claims budget
buyer: Facilities / Maintenance Manager of a convenience or supermarket chain
industry: Convenience stores, supermarkets and shopping-centre units with automatic pedestrian doors
current_workaround: Six-monthly contractor service, reactive breakdown call-outs, and paper daily checks, if any.
sensor_concept: Retrofit puck on the door leaf with an accelerometer (cycle count, closing speed/deceleration, impacts), a current clamp on the operator supply (motor strain, stalled door) and a reed contact for 'door closed after hours'. NB-IoT. Condition-based service alerts, a 'door open after closing' alarm and an automatic daily-check record.
notes: c1: injury claims. c2: daily use and checks. c4: BS EN 16005/DHF guidance plus insurer security. c6: automatic-door maintainers (DHF members) visit on contract and would resell. c7: OEM connectivity exists only on new doors, so a multi-brand retrofit is a gap. c8: accelerometer plus clamp.

title: High-street shop basement stockrooms flood when a sump pump fails or its float jams in a storm
problem: Many town-centre shops keep stock in waterproofed (Type C cavity drain) basements drained by sump pumps. A pump failure, jammed float or tripped supply during heavy rain floods the stockroom overnight (~£10k–£50k of stock plus closure), and insurers may argue lack of maintenance. BS 8102 expects pumped systems to be maintained and alarmed, but the alarm is usually a local buzzer that nobody hears after closing.
who_suffers: Shop owner and staff; the landlord
buyer: Owner/Operations Manager of an independent retailer or small chain, or the landlord's managing agent
industry: High-street shops and restaurants with pumped basement stockrooms
current_workaround: Annual pump service by the waterproofing contractor, a local high-level buzzer, and staff checking on arrival.
sensor_concept: High-water float switch, current clamp on each pump (running, stalled, short-cycling) and power-loss detection. LTE-M with battery backup, since basements lack Wi-Fi. Out-of-hours alerts, plus a run-hour log that tells the contractor when to service.
notes: c1: basement stock losses. c4: BS 8102 maintenance expectation and insurer scrutiny. c6: basement waterproofing contractors sell annual pump service contracts and would resell. c8: float plus clamp. c7 risk: some pump makers sell basic GSM alarm units.

title: Convenience-store remote condensing units leak refrigerant slowly until the chillers fail on a hot weekend
problem: Independent and symbol-group convenience stores run chiller cabinets off remote condensing units. A slow refrigerant leak only shows when cabinets warm up, typically on the hottest weekend. The store then loses ~£5k–£15k of chilled stock and pays for an emergency engineer and ~£1k+ of high-GWP refrigerant. F-gas rules require periodic leak checks and records, which a contractor does every 3–12 months.
who_suffers: Store owners; staff binning stock
buyer: Owner/Operator of 2–20 convenience stores (Spar, Londis, Nisa, Costcutter retailers)
industry: Independent and symbol-group convenience stores and forecourt shops
current_workaround: Staff reading cabinet thermometers, scheduled F-gas leak-check visits and reactive breakdown calls.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on each condensing unit (compressor duty cycle, short-cycling) plus clamp-on pipe temperature sensors on the suction and liquid lines. NB-IoT. Trend analysis flags rising run-time or falling subcooling weeks before failure, and the data feeds the F-gas leak-check record.
notes: c1: stock plus refrigerant cost. c4: F-gas leak-check records. c6: refrigeration contractors already visit quarterly. c8: clamps only, no refrigerant gas sensor. c7 risk: cabinet temperature monitoring is crowded, so position this as leak prediction for SME stores.

title: Unattended night deliveries leave convenience-store back doors unsecured and chilled cages warming in the stockroom
problem: Wholesalers and symbol groups deliver to many convenience stores overnight using door codes or keys. Drivers sometimes leave the back door unlocked or the alarm unset, or leave chilled and frozen cages outside the cold room. The store then opens to theft, an insurer security-warranty breach or ~£1k–£5k of stock to bin, and the dispute over who left what open is settled by guesswork. Across an estate this happens weekly.
who_suffers: Store owners and managers; wholesaler delivery teams
buyer: Retail Operations Director of a multi-site convenience retailer, or Logistics Manager at a convenience wholesaler running unattended deliveries
industry: Convenience stores receiving unattended overnight deliveries
current_workaround: Alarm-system open/close reports, driver sign-off sheets and CCTV review after the fact.
sensor_concept: Door contacts on the delivery door and cold-room door, a PIR in the drop zone and an air-temperature probe at the cage drop point. LTE-M. Alert if the door is left open or unlocked after the delivery ends, or if cages sit at ambient for more than 30 minutes. Time-stamped proof-of-delivery record for both parties.
notes: c2: nightly. c5: multi-site retailer or wholesaler owns the loss. c6: the wholesaler already visits nightly and could bundle it. c8: contacts, PIR and temperature. c1 and c7 are moderate.

title: Garden-centre plant-area irrigation fails during a hot weekend and thousands of pounds of stock wilts
problem: Garden centres hold ~£50k–£250k of outdoor plants on benches watered by drip, capillary or overhead irrigation. A stuck solenoid, empty break tank, tripped pump or timer fault during a heatwave weekend can kill, or make unsaleable, ~£5k–£20k of stock by Monday. A valve stuck open wastes metered water instead.
who_suffers: Plant-area staff and managers; the business's margin
buyer: Plant Area Manager / Store Manager at a garden-centre group or large independent
industry: Garden centres and plant retailers with automated bench irrigation
current_workaround: Staff hand-watering at weekends, timer controllers and walking the benches.
sensor_concept: Pulse flow meter and pressure switch on each irrigation zone, a float on the break tank and a capacitive moisture sensor in sentinel pots. LoRaWAN. Alert when a zone fails to flow on schedule, flows continuously, or pots dry out in a heatwave.
notes: c1: stock losses. c2: weekly in summer. c5: group plant manager with budget. c6: irrigation installers service annually. c8: flow and float are simple. c4 is weak (no rule).

title: Smouldering fires after hot works on historic roofs: the 60-minute fire watch is unprovable and the roof void is unwatched overnight
problem: Lead-roofing, plumbing and torch-on work on historic buildings is a classic cause of catastrophic heritage fires (Uppark, 1989, was started by a contractor's blowlamp on the roof). The Joint Code of Practice on fire prevention on construction sites and insurers' hot-work permits require at least 60 minutes of fire watch after work stops, with later checks. In a void of dry historic timber, though, a smoulder can break out hours later after the site is locked. Losses run to £m, and a contractor that cannot show the permit conditions were met faces uninsured liability.
who_suffers: Owners of heritage buildings, conservation contractors and their insurers
buyer: Contracts Manager / Managing Director of a heritage roofing, leadwork or conservation contractor
industry: Conservation roofing, leadwork and building contractors working on listed buildings, churches and historic houses
current_workaround: Paper hot-work permits, operatives standing fire watch for an hour, sometimes temporary site fire alarms. FM-approved remote fire-watch systems exist but are camera-based, US/industrial and costly.
sensor_concept: Clip-on battery node with an 8x8 thermopile array (AMG8833-class, not a camera) aimed at the work area, plus a rate-of-rise heat sensor and an optical smoke sensor. LTE-M. Logs the 60-minute watch, then keeps monitoring for 12–24 hours after works, alerting the site manager and keyholder. Hired per day, with a permit-compliance PDF.
notes: c1: £m heritage fire losses. c4: JCOP and insurer hot-work conditions. c5: the contractor owns permit compliance and liability. c6: heritage insurers and roofing/scaffold suppliers already serve these jobs. c7: incumbents are camera-based enterprise kit. c8: thermopile, smoke and LTE-M are cheap.

title: Bronze sculptures, lead statues and stone urns lifted from country-house gardens and sculpture parks overnight
problem: Outdoor statuary is stolen to order or for scrap. A Henry Moore bronze valued at ~£3m was taken from the Henry Moore Foundation in 2005 and is believed to have been melted down. Lead garden statues and antique urns (~£5k–£100k each) regularly vanish from estates. Specialist fine-art and heritage insurers impose security conditions on outdoor works, but grounds are far too large for conventional intruder alarms.
who_suffers: Owners of historic houses and estates, sculpture parks and garden-antiques dealers; their insurers
buyer: Estate Manager / Owner of a privately owned historic house run as a visitor or wedding business, or Collections Manager of a commercial sculpture park
industry: Privately owned historic houses, sculpture parks and garden-antiques dealers
current_workaround: Bolting or anchoring in concrete, forensic marking, occasional CCTV near the house, and night patrols on larger estates.
sensor_concept: Puck bonded under or inside the plinth with an accelerometer/tilt sensor to detect lifting, cutting or tilting. LoRaWAN to an estate gateway, or LTE-M. Instant alerts to keyholders via an alarm-receiving centre, plus a monthly status report for the insurer.
notes: c1: very high per-incident values. c4: insurer security conditions. c5: estate owners run businesses with budgets. c6: heritage/fine-art insurers' surveyors already visit. c8: tilt plus LPWAN. Weak on c2 (rare per site).

title: Fine-art vans left unattended at services or loading bays, breaching loan conditions and losing theft cover
problem: Museum loan agreements, Government Indemnity Scheme conditions and fine-art transit policies typically require works in transit to travel in alarmed, climate-controlled vehicles that are never left unattended, usually with two crew. Thefts from vans parked at services or outside venues can involve ~£50k to £m of objects and are refused or disputed if the vehicle was left. Lenders also demand a journey report, which the shipper reconstructs from memory and paper.
who_suffers: Lending museums and collectors, fine-art shippers and couriers
buyer: Operations Director / Head of Transport at a fine-art logistics company
industry: Fine-art shipping and handling firms serving museums, galleries and auction houses
current_workaround: Two-person crews, generic vehicle trackers, separate temperature/RH loggers in the cargo bay and paper courier reports.
sensor_concept: Cab occupancy sensor (mmWave radar/PIR), cargo-door reed contacts, cargo-bay temperature/RH and shock sensors, and GPS. LTE-M. Alert if the cab is empty with the engine off while a loan is aboard. Automatic per-journey compliance report (attended time, door openings, climate) for lenders and insurers.
notes: c1: high object values. c4: GIS/loan-agreement and insurer unattended-vehicle conditions. c5: the shipper owns the liability. c6: museum registrars and fine-art insurers already demand reports. c7: trackers and loggers exist separately, but no attendance-compliance product. c8: all off-the-shelf parts.

title: Overfired wood-burners and unswept flues set thatched holiday cottages and pubs alight
problem: Fire services attribute most thatch fires to chimneys and wood-burners: sparks, or a flue run too hot, ignite the thatch. A thatch fire typically costs ~£250k–£1m+ and can destroy a listed building. Specialist thatch insurers require annual sweeping, spark arrestors and sensible use. Owners of holiday lets and pubs, however, cannot see how hard guests and staff run the stove.
who_suffers: Owners of thatched holiday lets and pubs; guests; insurers
buyer: Owner/Operator of a thatched holiday-let portfolio, or Estates Manager at a pub company with thatched pubs
industry: Thatched listed holiday cottages, pubs and inns
current_workaround: Annual chimney sweep certificate, spark arrestor, house rules for guests, and magnetic stove-pipe thermometers that nobody reads.
sensor_concept: Thermocouple strap on the flue pipe (MAX31855-class interface) with LTE-M. Alerts on overfiring and chimney-fire temperature signatures, counts burn hours so the sweep is booked on actual usage, and produces an insurer report of sweeping and safe use.
notes: c1: high loss per fire. c4: insurer sweeping conditions. c6: chimney sweeps (HETAS/NACS) visit yearly, and thatch insurers/brokers could subsidise. c8: thermocouple plus cellular is cheap. c5 is weaker for single-cottage owners.

title: Listed buildings next to basement digs and demolitions: party-wall awards demand crack and tilt readings taken by hand
problem: Party-wall awards and planning conditions for works next to listed or historic buildings commonly require crack and tilt monitoring of the neighbour for the duration of the works. Surveyors visit monthly or fortnightly to read tell-tale gauges and level points (~£200–£500 a visit). Movement between visits goes unseen, and damage claims (~£10k–£100k+) are argued over without a continuous record.
who_suffers: Owners of the adjoining listed building; the developer; the basement or demolition contractor
buyer: Project Manager at a basement/refurbishment contractor, or the developer paying for monitoring under the party-wall award
industry: Basement construction and refurbishment next to listed terraces and heritage buildings (London and historic towns)
current_workaround: Manual tell-tale and precise-levelling readings by monitoring surveyors. Wireless structural monitoring (tiltmeters, crack meters) is used only on large projects.
sensor_concept: Battery crack-displacement sensor (linear potentiometer bridging the crack) plus a MEMS tilt sensor on the façade. LoRaWAN/LTE-M, reading hourly. Alerts at the trigger levels set in the award, and a monthly report for both party-wall surveyors.
notes: c2: monthly duty. c3: paid surveyor visits. c4: award or planning condition. c5: contractor/developer pays. c6: party-wall surveyors and monitoring firms already visit. c7: enterprise wireless monitoring is priced for major projects. c8: potentiometer plus MEMS tilt.

title: Temporary roofs over historic buildings under restoration lift or overflow in storms, pouring rain onto exposed interiors
problem: When a historic roof is stripped for re-leading or re-slating, a scaffold temporary roof or sheeting protects the interior for months. In gales the sheets lift or temporary gutters overflow, and water reaches decorative plaster ceilings, panelling and contents (~£50k–£500k+ claims under works or existing-structures insurance). Temporary works are inspected weekly and after storms, but the damage happens overnight.
who_suffers: Owners of historic buildings, conservation main contractors and scaffold contractors
buyer: Contracts Manager at a heritage main contractor, or at the scaffold contractor providing the temporary roof
industry: Heritage restoration projects under scaffold temporary roofs
current_workaround: Weekly scaffold inspections, after-storm visits, and buckets and polythene.
sensor_concept: Hire kit: water-presence sensors at low points on exposed ceilings and attic floors, float switches in temporary gutters, and accelerometer/tilt nodes on temporary roof sheets, plus a site anemometer. LTE-M. Storm alerts to the contractor's on-call manager, with time-stamped evidence for insurers.
notes: c1: high claims. c5: contractor owns the risk. c6: scaffold contractors already inspect weekly. c8: simple sensors. c7: generic water sensors exist, but there is no heritage temporary-works hire product. c2: storms several times per winter.

title: Frost kills fresh lime mortar and plaster on winter heritage repairs, and the contractor can't show it was protected
problem: Lime pointing, render and plaster on listed buildings must be protected from frost and rapid drying while they cure, and specifications typically forbid work, or demand protection, below ~5°C. One frosty night under inadequate hessian can blow fresh lime work, which then has to be raked out and redone (~£5k–£50k on a large elevation). Clients and conservation officers then dispute who pays, because nobody recorded conditions at the wall face overnight.
who_suffers: Heritage masonry and plastering contractors; building owners
buyer: Contracts Manager / Owner of a heritage masonry, lime-plastering or conservation contractor
industry: Conservation masonry and lime-plastering contractors on listed buildings and churches
current_workaround: Weather forecasts, hessian and polythene sheeting, occasional site heaters and morning inspections, with nothing recorded overnight.
sensor_concept: Clip-on scaffold nodes with an air temperature/RH sensor and a contact thermistor on the wall face behind the sheeting. LTE-M, battery powered, as hire kits. Frost-risk alert in the evening, to add protection or heaters, and a time-stamped curing-conditions record per elevation for the client and conservation officer.
notes: c1: costly rework and disputes. c2: nightly risk through winter. c4: specification and contract requirements. c5: the contractor owns the rework cost. c6: lime suppliers and scaffolders already serve these jobs. c8: temperature/RH only. c7: no product targets lime-curing evidence.

title: Livery-yard horses escape onto roads through gates left open by liveries or through dead electric fencing
problem: On DIY and part-livery yards dozens of owners use the same field and yard gates, and electric fences short out on wet grass or fallen branches. Loose horses on roads cause collisions; keepers can be held strictly liable under the Animals Act 1971, and claims run to ~£100k–£1m+ (injuries, vehicles, horses destroyed). Yard owners are expected to check fencing and gates daily, and their liability insurers ask about it.
who_suffers: Yard owners, horse owners and motorists
buyer: Owner/Proprietor of a commercial livery yard or equestrian centre (20–80 horses)
industry: Commercial livery yards and equestrian centres
current_workaround: 'Shut the gate' signs, padlocks and yard rules, walking fence lines daily with a fence tester, and Wi-Fi energisers only near the house.
sensor_concept: Gate nodes with reed/tilt sensors (alert if open more than 5 minutes) and electric-fence line monitors (pulse detection through a high-voltage divider) at the far end of each paddock line. LoRaWAN gateway at the yard, or LTE-M nodes. Alerts to the yard manager's phone, plus a daily fence/gate check record for insurers.
notes: c1: high liability claims. c2: daily checks. c4: Animals Act liability and insurer questions. c5: the yard proprietor owns the liability. c6: equine liability insurers and fencing/energiser dealers. c8: reed/tilt plus pulse detector. c7: farm fence monitors exist, but few target livery yards.

title: A stabled horse stops drinking overnight and colic is only noticed at morning feed: £5k–£10k surgery or a dead horse
problem: A drop in water intake is one of the earliest signs of colic, but automatic drinkers give staff no idea how much each horse drank. Colic surgery costs ~£5k–£10k and is among the largest categories of equine insurance claim. At racing and competition yards, a horse lost or off work costs far more. Welfare codes expect water to be checked at least twice daily.
who_suffers: Horses, owners, yard managers and equine insurers
buyer: Head Lad / Yard Manager at a racing yard, or Proprietor of a full-livery or competition yard
industry: Racing yards and full-livery or competition yards fitted with automatic drinkers
current_workaround: Buckets instead of automatic drinkers so staff can eyeball intake, plus evening and late-night checks. A couple of small vendors (HydraSure, Cascada) sell their own smart drinkers rather than retrofits for existing fittings.
sensor_concept: Inline Hall-effect pulse flow meter (~£5) on each stable drinker feed with a LoRaWAN node. Builds a per-horse daily intake baseline and alerts on a sharp overnight drop or no flow (frozen or blocked drinker). Weekly intake report for vets and owners.
notes: c1: colic surgery cost. c2: daily. c5: yard proprietor or head lad. c6: equine vets visit yards weekly, and equine insurers pay the colic claims. c8: flow meter plus LPWAN. c7: two small own-hardware incumbents leave a retrofit gap.

title: Commercial horse transporters can't evidence in-transit temperatures and journeys, and horses arrive with shipping fever
problem: Heat and poor air in a closed horse lorry cause heat stress and transport-associated pleuropneumonia ('shipping fever') in horses worth ~£20k to £1m+. Animal transport rules (Regulation (EC) 1/2005 as retained, WATO 2006) require transporter authorisation and, for long journeys of unregistered horses, temperature monitoring, recording and navigation records. Owners and insurers of registered sport horses and racehorses increasingly expect the same evidence. Many lorries have only a cab thermometer.
who_suffers: Horses and owners; commercial transporters and their insurers
buyer: Owner/Managing Director of a commercial horse transport company (Type 1/Type 2 authorised)
industry: Commercial equine transport (racing, sport-horse and bloodstock shipping)
current_workaround: Cab dial thermometers, paper journey logs and driver judgement on vents. Integrated systems come only on new high-end lorries.
sensor_concept: Temperature/humidity sensors at horse head height in each bay, an accelerometer on partitions (horse down or scrambling) and GPS. LTE-M. Driver alerts in the cab via a phone app, plus an automatic journey log and temperature record for APHA, export paperwork and owners.
notes: c4: named statutory recording requirement (partial coverage). c1: high horse values. c5: transporter owns authorisation and claims. c6: horsebox builders and coachbuilders fit kit. c8: off-the-shelf parts. c7 risk: builders fit systems on new lorries, but the retrofit market looks open.

title: Horseboxes run over their plated weight once horses and kit are aboard, bringing DVSA prohibitions, fines and void insurance
problem: 3.5t and 7.5t horseboxes are easily overloaded once horses, water, tack and living kit are aboard. DVSA roadside checks issue prohibitions and fines, and an overweight vehicle can invalidate insurance after a crash. Horsebox hire firms and commercial transporters carry the operator liability but cannot see what hirers or drivers load.
who_suffers: Horsebox hire firms, commercial transporters, drivers and horses
buyer: Owner of a horsebox hire business, or Transport Manager of a commercial equine transporter
industry: Horsebox hire and commercial equine transport (3.5t–7.5t vehicles)
current_workaround: Weighbridge visits when convenient, payload tables, and warnings in the hire T&Cs.
sensor_concept: Ride-height distance sensors (ToF/ultrasonic) between chassis and axle, calibrated once at a weighbridge, plus LTE-M/GPS. In-cab and app warning when the estimated gross weight exceeds the plate, and a trip-level weight record for hire disputes and DVSA.
notes: c4: DVSA enforcement. c5: hire firm or operator owns the liability. c6: horsebox dealers and builders. c8 weak spot: needs per-vehicle calibration. c7: on-board weighing exists for vans but is not marketed to horsebox hire.

title: Stable-block fires start at night on unmanned yards, where dust-triggered false alarms mean smoke alarms get unplugged
problem: Electrical faults, heaters, rug dryers, hay and bedding start stable fires that kill horses and destroy buildings (~£50k–£500k+ per fire). Domestic smoke detectors false-alarm constantly in dusty stables and get removed, and many yards have nobody on site overnight. Yard insurers and equine welfare bodies recommend detection suited to stables.
who_suffers: Horses, yard owners, livery clients and insurers
buyer: Proprietor of a livery or competition yard, or racing Yard Manager
industry: Livery, racing and competition yards with timber or barn stabling
current_workaround: No detection, or wired heat detectors only in large new barns; staff night checks; CCTV.
sensor_concept: Node in each stable aisle combining a rate-of-rise heat sensor and an electrochemical CO sensor (CO detects smouldering bedding without dust false alarms). LoRaWAN or LTE-M, battery powered. Escalating phone alerts to on-call staff and neighbours, plus a monthly self-test record for insurers.
notes: c1: high losses. c4: insurer recommendations. c5: yard owner. c6: equine insurers and agricultural electricians. c8: heat plus CO is cheap. c7: some stable-specific alarms exist, but few cheap wireless ones.

title: Horse walkers keep turning when a horse slips or is cast, and the racing yard finds the injury when staff come back
problem: Racing and competition yards put 4–6 horses at a time on mechanical horse walkers, often left for 30–60 minutes. If a horse slips, turns or is cast against a panel, the walker keeps pushing, causing injuries and occasionally deaths (vet bills ~£2k–£10k, and lost racehorse value far beyond that).
who_suffers: Horses, trainers and owners
buyer: Racehorse Trainer / Yard Manager
industry: Racing and competition yards using mechanical horse walkers
current_workaround: Stable staff checking periodically, CCTV, and built-in overload trips on some newer walkers.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the walker drive motor (torque spike when a horse resists or is down) plus an accelerometer on a divider panel (impacts). LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Immediate phone alert, and a run log for every session.
notes: c1: horse values. c2: daily use. c5: the trainer owns the loss. c6: walker installers and servicers. c8: clamp plus accelerometer. c4 is weak (no rule).

title: Buried pipes to paddock troughs leak for months at studs and livery yards: £5k+ water bills and dry troughs
problem: Studs and large livery yards run hundreds of metres of buried alkathene to field troughs. A split pipe or stuck ballcock can lose tens of cubic metres a day unnoticed, producing water bills of ~£5k–£20k before the next meter read, while horses in that field may be left without water. Non-household water retailers grant leak allowances only on proof of prompt repair.
who_suffers: Stud and yard owners; horses
buyer: Owner / Stud Manager of a stud farm or large livery yard
industry: Stud farms, large livery yards and equestrian centres with field troughs
current_workaround: Quarterly or estimated bills, walking the fields, and isolating sections to find leaks.
sensor_concept: Pulse reader clipped onto the existing water meter (reed or magnetometer pick-up), LTE-M/LoRaWAN. Night-flow leak detection, daily consumption trend and spike alerts, with optional trough float switches in remote fields.
notes: c1: water bill shocks. c2: continuous. c5: the owner pays the bill. c6: water retailers and agricultural plumbers. c8: meter pulse readers are cheap. c7 risk: some water retailers sell data loggers.

title: Dental suction motors and compressors fail mid-list in older practices, cancelling whole days of patients
problem: A failed wet-suction motor, compressor or air dryer stops every surgery in the practice. For a 4–6 chair practice a lost day is ~£5k–£10k of production, plus handpiece damage from wet air. Most practice compressors are pressure systems needing a PSSR written scheme and daily draining, and HTM 01-05 requires daily suction cleaning, but all these checks are manual. OEM remote monitoring (Dürr VistaSoft Monitor, DentalEZ Aeras, Air Techniques) only covers the maker's own newer units, not the mixed legacy plant in most UK practices.
who_suffers: Dentists, nurses and patients; the practice owner
buyer: Practice Owner/Principal, or Facilities/Compliance Manager at a dental group (e.g. Bupa Dental Care, mydentist, Portman, Rodericks)
industry: General dental practices with plant-room compressors and suction units
current_workaround: Annual service and PSSR inspection by independent dental engineers, nurses draining compressors and cleaning suction daily, and emergency call-outs.
sensor_concept: Current clamps on suction and compressor motors (duty cycle, start counts, overcurrent), a pressure transducer on the receiver, and temperature/humidity in the plant cupboard. LTE-M. Alerts on air leaks (rising duty cycle), overheating and missed drains, plus usage-based service tickets to the engineer.
notes: c1: lost production days. c4: PSSR and HTM 01-05 duties. c5: corporate dental groups have facilities budgets. c6: independent dental engineers already visit yearly. c7: OEM-only incumbents leave legacy mixed estates unserved. c8: clamps plus a pressure transducer.

title: Vet anaesthetic scavenging left off or failing exposes nurses to isoflurane between annual tests
problem: Vet practices run general anaesthetics daily. Active scavenging (AGSS) fans get switched off, ducts disconnect or flows drop, exposing nurses, including pregnant staff, to isoflurane above the workplace exposure limit. COSHH requires effective control, periodic thorough examination of the system and exposure monitoring, and RCVS Practice Standards assessors check it. Personal dosimetry is done once a year at best.
who_suffers: Veterinary nurses and surgeons; practice owners
buyer: Clinical Director / Group Health & Safety Manager at a veterinary group (e.g. IVC Evidensia, CVS, Medivet, Linnaeus)
industry: Small-animal veterinary practices and hospitals
current_workaround: Annual AGSS/LEV test by a contractor, annual personal badge sampling, and nurses glancing at the flow indicator.
sensor_concept: Differential pressure sensor in the scavenging duct, a current clamp on the AGSS fan, and an oxygen-flowmeter on/off sensor at the anaesthetic machine to detect 'GA in progress'. LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Alert when anaesthesia runs with scavenging off or under-flowing, and a monthly COSHH record per theatre.
notes: c2: daily GA. c4: COSHH and RCVS PSS. c5: vet group H&S has budget. c6: anaesthetic-machine and AGSS service engineers visit annually. c8: DP sensor plus clamp. c1 is weak (claims are rare).

title: Second-hand MRI scanners at vet referral centres: a chiller or cold-head compressor trips at the weekend and the helium boils off
problem: Veterinary referral hospitals often run refurbished superconducting MRI systems without the manufacturer's remote-monitoring service contract. If the chiller or cold-head compressor stops over a weekend (power blip, water-flow fault), liquid helium boils off and the magnet can quench. Helium refill and re-ramping cost ~£30k–£100k+, and the scanner is out of action for days to weeks while referrals go elsewhere.
who_suffers: Referral hospital clinicians and owners; patients awaiting scans
buyer: Hospital Director / Head of Diagnostic Imaging at a veterinary referral centre or vet group
industry: Veterinary referral hospitals running MRI
current_workaround: Local compressor alarm lamps, staff checks on weekdays, and third-party service contracts with periodic visits.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the cold-head compressor, temperature sensors on chilled-water flow and return, a flow switch and mains-loss detection, all installed outside the RF-shielded room. LTE-M. Immediate alerts to on-call staff and the service engineer, plus a run log for the service contract.
notes: c1: very high per incident. c5: hospital director with budget. c6: independent MRI service companies already visit. c7: OEM monitoring only comes with OEM contracts. c8: clamps plus temperature sensors. c2 is the weakness (rare events).

title: Controlled-drug cabinets in vet and dental-sedation practices are opened with no record that matches the register
problem: Ketamine, methadone and midazolam go missing from practice CD cabinets. Stock is reconciled against the register only periodically, so diversion surfaces weeks later and leads to RCVS/GDC proceedings, police involvement and dismissals. Practices must keep CDs in a locked cabinet with a running register, and practice-standards and CQC inspectors check stock and records.
who_suffers: Practice owners and clinical directors; honest staff under suspicion
buyer: Clinical Director / Compliance Manager at a veterinary or dental group
industry: Veterinary practices and dental practices offering IV sedation
current_workaround: Key-holder logs, weekly or monthly stock checks, and CCTV in some dispensaries. Electronic CD cabinets cost thousands.
sensor_concept: Reed contact on the CD cabinet door, an accelerometer for forced entry, and an optional NFC fob tap by the person opening it. LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Time-stamped opening log reconciled against register entries, with alerts for out-of-hours or unrecorded openings.
notes: c4: CD storage and register rules. c2: daily openings. c5: group compliance budget. c8: trivially cheap. c1 is the weak spot (losses are mostly regulatory).

title: Vet practices run out of oxygen mid-anaesthetic because nobody saw the cylinder bank empty
problem: Small-animal practices run every general anaesthetic on oxygen from cylinders on the machine or a small manifold. When the duty cylinder empties and the reserve is low or shut, nurses scramble mid-procedure. The result is a patient-safety incident and potential negligence claim (~£2k–£20k), plus emergency deliveries. Practice standards require the anaesthetic machine and gas supply to be checked before each list.
who_suffers: Vet nurses, surgeons and patients
buyer: Practice Manager / Clinical Director at an independent practice or vet group
industry: Small-animal veterinary practices using cylinder oxygen
current_workaround: Pre-list machine checks, reading gauges by eye, and keeping spare cylinders.
sensor_concept: Load-cell cradle under each cylinder estimating contents by weight, so nothing is fitted to the medical gas line, plus LoRaWAN/LTE-M. Low-contents and reorder alerts, and a pre-list check record per theatre.
notes: c2: daily use. c6: gas suppliers deliver weekly and could bundle it. c8: load cell plus LPWAN. c1 and c4 are moderate.

title: Hourly metal-detector tests at small food producers are back-filled on paper, and a detector that failed its test keeps running
problem: HACCP and BRCGS/SALSA require metal detectors to be challenged with ferrous, non-ferrous and stainless test pieces at set intervals (typically hourly, at start-up and at changeovers), with rejects confirmed into a locked bin. In small factories tests are skipped on busy shifts and ticked later, and auditors frequently raise non-conformities. A metal-contamination recall costs a small producer ~£20k–£200k plus possible delisting. Digital self-test systems come only with new premium detectors.
who_suffers: Line operators, technical managers, and the business that recalls
buyer: Technical Manager / Owner of an SME food manufacturer (SALSA or BRCGS certified)
industry: SME bakeries, ready-meal, snack, meat and confectionery producers with legacy metal detectors
current_workaround: Paper hourly test sheets, supervisor sign-off, and annual detector validation by the service engineer.
sensor_concept: Retrofit box wired to the detector's dry-contact outputs (detect/reject/fault). NFC-tagged test wands are read at the aperture so each test-piece type is logged, an IR beam in the reject bin confirms rejects arrive, and a reed contact sits on the bin lock. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT. Missed-test alerts to the supervisor, and an audit-ready CCP record.
notes: c2: hourly duty. c3: labour-heavy paper checks. c4: HACCP/BRCGS/SALSA CCP records. c5: technical manager owns audit and recall. c6: detector service engineers visit yearly. c7: OEM digital testing only on new high-end units. c8: contacts, NFC and IR beam.

title: High-care rooms lose positive air pressure unnoticed between once-a-shift gauge readings, raising Listeria risk in ready-to-eat food
problem: Ready-to-eat producers (sandwiches, salads, cooked meats) must keep high-care/high-risk areas supplied with filtered air at positive pressure relative to low-care areas, under BRCGS high-risk zone requirements. A failed fan, clogged filter or propped door reverses the airflow. Pressure is read off a dial gauge once a shift. Listeria outbreaks linked to RTE producers, such as the 2019 hospital-sandwich outbreak, led to closures and recalls costing £100ks.
who_suffers: Consumers (especially vulnerable ones), technical teams and the producer
buyer: Technical / Hygiene Manager at an SME ready-to-eat food manufacturer
industry: Chilled ready-to-eat producers: sandwiches, salads, cooked meats and ready meals
current_workaround: Daily manual gauge readings on paper and quarterly air-handling service. BMS monitoring exists only on large sites.
sensor_concept: Digital differential-pressure sensor (Sensirion SDP-class) across each high-care wall or door, plus door contacts. LoRaWAN. Alarm if the differential collapses for more than N minutes, and a continuous record for BRCGS auditors and EHOs.
notes: c2/c3: daily manual readings. c4: BRCGS high-risk requirements. c5: technical manager. c6: HVAC maintainers visit quarterly. c8: cheap DP sensor. c1 is indirect (via outbreak risk).

title: Fryer and oven extract ducts in food factories are cleaned on a guessed schedule, and insurers refuse fire claims without TR19 proof
problem: Grease builds up in extract ductwork over frying ranges, ovens and smokehouses. TR19 Grease (BESA) sets cleaning frequency by hours of use, and insurers make TR19 cleaning a policy condition. One insurer reportedly refused a ~£2m hotel fire claim for lack of deep-clean records, and ombudsman cases turn on fryer-duct cleaning. Food factories running two or three shifts slip past the interval because nobody tracks actual usage hours.
who_suffers: Factory owners, engineering managers and insurers
buyer: Engineering Manager / Owner of an SME food manufacturer with frying, roasting or baking lines
industry: Food manufacturers with fryer, oven and smokehouse extract systems (snacks, fried foods, bakery, meat)
current_workaround: Fixed-interval TR19 cleans by a duct-hygiene contractor (~£500–£3k per clean) with certificates on file, but no record of real usage hours.
sensor_concept: Current clamp or vibration sensor on each extract fan for run-hours, plus a duct-surface temperature sensor as an over-temperature/fire precursor. LTE-M/LoRaWAN. Calculates the TR19 cleaning due date from actual hours and books the contractor, alerts on duct over-temperature, and keeps an insurer-ready history.
notes: c4: insurer TR19 condition, with refused-claim evidence. c1: high fire losses. c6: TR19 duct-cleaning contractors (VHR register) visit every 3–12 months and would resell. c8: clamp plus thermistor. c7: no usage-based product seen.

title: Knife sterilisers in meat cutting plants drift below 82°C mid-shift, triggering FSA audit non-compliances
problem: Approved meat establishments must provide tool sterilisers supplied with water at not less than 82°C, or an equivalent system. Kettles get topped up with cold water, elements fail or units are switched off. Official veterinarians record the shortfall, which affects the plant's audit outcome, audit frequency and FSA charges. After E. coli or Salmonella findings, product is held (~£5k–£50k). Operators currently dip a thermometer a few times a shift.
who_suffers: Plant operators, technical managers and consumers
buyer: Technical Manager / Plant Manager of an FSA-approved cutting plant or small abattoir
industry: FSA-approved meat cutting plants, small abattoirs and game-handling establishments
current_workaround: Manual thermometer checks recorded on paper 2–4 times a shift, plus OV spot checks.
sensor_concept: Sealed stainless temperature probe clipped into each steriliser, with LoRaWAN, since steel-clad cold rooms make Wi-Fi unreliable. Alert below 82°C for more than N minutes, and a per-steriliser HACCP record for the OV and FSA audit.
notes: c2: several checks per shift. c4: legal temperature with an audit regime. c5: plant technical manager. c6: hygiene-chemical suppliers and plant engineers visit weekly. c8: simple immersion temperature probe. c1 is moderate.

title: Small dairies' batch-pasteuriser chart recorders jam or run out of ink, so the batch can't be released
problem: Farm dairies, ice-cream makers and cheesemakers pasteurising in vats must be able to show each batch reached time and temperature, normally via an automatic recorder. Paper chart recorders jam, lose pens or drift, and a batch without a valid record has to be held or discarded (~£1k–£5k a batch). Missing records are a standard EHO/FSA finding. Paperless recorders cost ~£1k+ installed and still need someone to watch them.
who_suffers: Dairy owners, cheesemakers and ice-cream makers
buyer: Owner/Operator of an on-farm dairy, artisan cheesemaker or ice-cream manufacturer
industry: On-farm dairies and artisan cheese and ice-cream producers using batch (vat) pasteurisation
current_workaround: Circular paper chart recorders, manual thermometer reads written up afterwards, and annual calibration.
sensor_concept: Calibrated PT100 probe in the vat thermowell plus agitator current sensing, LTE-M. Time-at-temperature record per batch, a real-time alert if holding temperature drops, and a signed digital batch chart for EHOs and customers.
notes: c4: recording requirement and inspections. c2: every batch. c5: owner-operator. c6: dairy equipment engineers and dairy consultants. c8: needs a traceable-calibrated PT100 (moderate). c7: paperless recorders exist but aren't cloud-connected or cheap.

title: Artisan smokehouse kilns overheat or flare overnight, causing smokery fires and leaving cold-smoked fish with no temperature record
problem: Smoke generators and wood-fired kilns run unattended overnight. Sawdust flare-ups and grease deposits cause smokehouse fires that can destroy premises (~£100k+). Cold-smoked salmon must be held below ~30°C during smoking to manage Listeria and C. botulinum risk, with records expected in the HACCP plan. Older and home-built kilns have no logging.
who_suffers: Smokery owners, staff and consumers
buyer: Owner/Operator of an artisan smokehouse or small smoked-fish/meat processor
industry: Artisan smokeries and small smoked fish, meat and cheese producers
current_workaround: Dial thermometers, staff checking kilns at night, and paper HACCP logs.
sensor_concept: Thermocouples in the kiln chamber and exhaust plus a door contact, LTE-M. Out-of-hours over-temperature fire alert, a cold-smoke temperature ceiling alarm, and a per-batch HACCP temperature record.
notes: c1: fire loss. c4: HACCP records plus insurer interest. c5: owner-operator. c8: thermocouple plus cellular. c7: modern kilns have controllers, but old and artisan kilns are unserved. c6 is weak (kiln suppliers only).

title: Failed underfloor heating beneath food-factory freezer stores lets frost heave crack the floor, causing six-figure repairs
problem: Freezer and blast-freezer stores sit on slabs with underfloor heating (glycol loops or electric mats) to stop the ground freezing. If the heating fails unnoticed for months, ice lenses lift the slab, racking goes out of plumb and the store must be emptied for repair (~£100k–£1m). Sub-floor temperatures are meant to be checked through probe tubes, but in SME factories nobody does it.
who_suffers: Factory owners, engineering teams and cold-store users
buyer: Engineering / Maintenance Manager of a food manufacturer with freezer stores
industry: Frozen-food manufacturers and processors with on-site freezer stores
current_workaround: Occasional manual readings of under-slab probes and refrigeration contractor checks. Nothing happens until the floor cracks.
sensor_concept: Thermistor strings dropped into the existing under-slab probe tubes, plus a current clamp on heater mats or the glycol pump. LoRaWAN. Alerts on a sub-zero subsoil trend or heater off, and a monthly record for insurers and the refrigeration contractor.
notes: c1: very high repair cost. c6: refrigeration contractors visit quarterly. c8: thermistor plus clamp. c2 (slow-developing, rare event) and c4 are weak.

title: Small food packers give away 2–4% extra product to stay legal on average weight, with paper ℮-mark records
problem: Packers using the ℮ mark must meet average-quantity rules and keep records of their checks under the Weights and Measures (Packaged Goods) Regulations 2006. Without checkweighers, small producers hand-weigh samples and deliberately overfill to be safe. A ~2% giveaway on £2m of output is ~£40k a year, and Trading Standards short-weight findings bring enforcement.
who_suffers: Owners and production staff
buyer: Owner / Operations Manager of an SME packer (bakery, confectionery, coffee, dried goods)
industry: SME food packers using manual or semi-automatic filling of ℮-marked prepacks
current_workaround: Bench scales, clipboard sample checks every 15–60 minutes and generous overfilling. Checkweighers (£10k+) are only on bigger lines.
sensor_concept: Retrofit load cell plus HX711 under an existing bench, or a cheap platform scale, with a LoRaWAN/cellular gateway (no factory Wi-Fi). Operators drop samples and the system logs weights, computes T1/T2 and average quantity per batch, alerts on drift and quantifies giveaway.
notes: c1: recurring giveaway money. c2: continuous sampling. c4: Packaged Goods Regulations records. c6: scale service companies (UKWF members) visit yearly for verification. c8: load cell. c7 risk: checkweigher software is crowded at the top end.

title: Food-factory effluent balancing tanks overflow when a pump trips at night, causing fish kills and EA prosecutions
problem: Dairies, meat plants and soft-drinks factories hold wash-water in balancing tanks or pump sumps before treatment or discharge to sewer. When a pump trips or level control sticks overnight, effluent overflows to surface-water drains and watercourses. Pollution prosecutions of food firms by the EA and water companies run from ~£10k to £1m+, and permits and consents require the system to be controlled.
who_suffers: Factory owners, environmental managers and the receiving river
buyer: Environmental / Engineering Manager of an SME food or soft-drinks manufacturer
industry: Dairies, meat processors, and soft-drink and juice producers with on-site effluent tanks
current_workaround: Local float alarms with a beacon and shift checks. Telemetry only on large sites.
sensor_concept: Float switches or a pressure level sensor in each sump or tank plus current clamps on transfer pumps, LTE-M. Out-of-hours alert on high level or pump fault, and a level and pump-run log as permit evidence.
notes: c1: prosecution fines. c4: permit/consent conditions with enforcement. c5: environmental manager. c6: tankering and effluent-treatment contractors. c8: float plus clamp. c7 risk: utility pumping-station telemetry incumbents.

title: Shellfish depuration tanks run with dead UV lamps or cold water, and norovirus outbreaks are traced back to the batch
problem: Live oysters, mussels and clams must be depurated in approved systems with working UV disinfection, adequate flow and a minimum water temperature for a minimum time, with batch records. A failed UV lamp or chiller makes depuration ineffective, and norovirus outbreaks lead to recalls, lost restaurant customers and harvesting restrictions (~£10k–£100k).
who_suffers: Shellfish producers, restaurants and consumers
buyer: Owner/Manager of a shellfish depuration centre or oyster farm
industry: Shellfish depuration and dispatch centres
current_workaround: Manual checks of the lamp-on indicator, thermometer and timer, written on batch sheets, with lamps replaced on the hour counter.
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the UV ballast, a temperature probe in the tank and a flow switch/pulse meter on recirculation, LTE-M. A button starts the batch timer. Alert on any fault mid-cycle, and an automatic batch record for food-authority inspections.
notes: c4: approval conditions with records. c2: every batch. c5: owner-operator. c8: clamp, temperature and flow. c7: likely unserved. c1 and c6 are moderate.

title: Small juice, dairy and soft-drink producers can't prove clean-in-place washes reached temperature and time
problem: Manual or semi-automatic CIP washes in small plants rely on operators, and a short or cool caustic cycle leaves biofilm. Product then spoils or is recalled (~£10k–£100k with retailer charge-backs). BRCGS/SALSA require cleaning to be validated and verified, and auditors ask for CIP records that small plants don't have.
who_suffers: Production teams and technical managers
buyer: Technical Manager / Owner of an SME juice, dairy or soft-drinks producer
industry: SME juice, smoothie, dairy and soft-drinks producers with manual CIP
current_workaround: Paper CIP sheets, operators reading dial thermometers, and ATP swabs after the clean.
sensor_concept: Clamp-on pipe temperature sensors on CIP return lines, a flow pulse meter and a current clamp on the CIP pump. LoRaWAN. Per-circuit record of time above set temperature, with alerts on short or cool washes.
notes: c2: daily washes. c4: cleaning validation requirement. c6: CIP chemical suppliers visit monthly. c8: clamp-on sensors only, no conductivity probe. c1 is moderate.
